events.ctx: Nanakshahi New Year (Pehla Chet) marks the beginning of the Sikh calendar year, introduced to synchronize historical Sikh events with the tropical solar calendar. Commencing on Chet 1 (March 14), it commemorates the era founded in honor of Guru Nanak Dev Ji (originating in 1469 CE). The day is celebrated globally with special Gurdwara gatherings, Asa Ki Vaar Kirtan, and recitations of the sacred Barah Maha composition from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Shaheed Bhagat Singh (1907–1931), the visionary Sikh revolutionary born in Banga, Lyallpur (now Pakistan). A passionate patriot who founded the Naujawan Bharat Sabha, he resisted British colonial imperialism with indomitable courage. Following the Lahore Conspiracy Case, he alongside Rajguru and Sukhdev embraced the gallows with smiles on March 23, 1931 in Lahore Central Jail at the tender age of 23, inspiring millions across India to rise against colonial tyranny.

When persecution renewed under Governor Yahya Khan, both father and son refused to renounce the Sikh faith despite being strapped to rotating wheels with sharp blades (Charkhari). They embraced martyrdom joyfully while reciting Gurbani.

The day aims to raise global awareness about the religious significance and sanctity of the Sikh turban.

The Guru himself laid the foundation and built the platform with the help of Bhai Gurdas Ji and Baba Buddha Ji, without employing any outside labor. It serves as the highest seat of decision-making for the Sikh community, where matters of political and social importance are addressed.

events.ctx: Guru Har Krishan Ji (1656-1664) was the eighth Sikh Guru who became Guru at the age of 5 and is remembered for his selfless service during a smallpox epidemic.

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Shaheed Udham Singh (1899-1940), the Sikh revolutionary who assassinated Michael O'Dwyer in London to avenge the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919. He was executed in London and is revered as a national hero.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਸ਼ਹੀਦ ਊਧਮ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
title.roman: Shaheedi Diwas Shaheed Udham Singh Ji
title.hindi: शहीदी दिवस शहीद ऊधम सिंह जी

events.ctx: The Guru Ka Bagh Morcha (1922) was a key event in the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Sikhs peacefully protested against Mahant Sundar Das, who had illegal control of Gurdwara Guru Ka Bagh. Despite brutal police beatings, Sikhs remained non-violent, eventually winning control of the Gurdwara and demonstrating the power of peaceful resistance.

title.gurmukhi: ਮੋਰਚਾ ਗੁਰੂ ਕਾ ਬਾਗ਼
title.roman: Morcha Guru Ka Bagh

events.ctx: Annual Jormela at Sri Baba Bakala Sahib, commemorating the historic revelation of the Ninth Sikh Guru, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, in 1664. Following the passing of Guru Har Krishan Sahib Ji with the words 'Baba Bakale', twenty-two imposter Sodhis set up seats claiming the Guruship. The wealthy merchant Makhan Shah Lubana, whose ship was saved in a sea storm by the Guru, arrived and tested each claimant with two gold dinars, discovering the true Guru in his subterranean meditation room (Bhora Sahib) and proclaiming from the rooftop: 'Guru Ladho Re' (The True Guru is Found!).

title.gurmukhi: ਜੋੜ ਮੇਲਾ ਬਾਬਾ ਬਕਾਲਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ (ਰੱਖੜ ਪੁੰਨਿਆ)
title.roman: Jor Mela Baba Bakala Sahib

events.ctx: India's Independence Day (August 15, 1947) commemorates the end of British colonial rule. Sikhs played a significant role in the freedom struggle, with many Sikh martyrs sacrificing their lives. However, the Partition that accompanied independence caused immense suffering to Sikhs and Punjab.

title.gurmukhi: ਭਾਰਤ ਦਾ ਸੁਤੰਤਰਤਾ ਦਿਵਸ
title.roman: Independence Day of India

events.ctx: Partition Prayer Day (Vibhajan Ardaas Divas) commemorates the tragic suffering, massacre, and catastrophic displacement endured by the Sikh community during the Partition of Punjab in August 1947. Millions of Sikhs were forced to abandon their ancestral lands, homes, and sacred historical shrines—including Gurdwara Janam Asthan Nankana Sahib, Sri Panja Sahib, and Gurdwara Dehra Sahib—in what became Pakistan, with hundreds of thousands martyred during the mass migration.

title.gurmukhi: ਦੇਸ਼ ਵੰਡ ਦੇ ਸ਼ਹੀਦਾਂ ਦੀ ਯਾਦ ਵਿਚ ਅਰਦਾਸ ਦਿਵਸ
title.roman: Partition Remembrance Day

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Sant Harchand Singh Longowal (1932–1985), prominent Sikh religious and political leader who served as President of the Shiromani Akali Dal and Dictator of the Dharam Yudh Morcha. Seeking a peaceful resolution to Punjab's political turmoil, he signed the historic Punjab Accord (Rajiv-Longowal Accord) in July 1985 and was assassinated shortly after while praying at Gurdwara Sherpur.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਸੰਤ ਹਰਚੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਲੌਂਗੋਵਾਲ
title.roman: Shaheedi Sant Harchand Singh Longowal
title.hindi: शहीदी दिवस संत हरचंद सिंह लोंगोवाल

events.ctx: Sampooranta Divas commemorates the completion of Guru Granth Sahib Ji. The final version was compiled by Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Damdama Sahib in 1706, adding the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji to the Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan Dev Ji. It is the eternal Guru of Sikhs.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਪੂਰਨਤਾ ਦਿਵਸ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ
title.roman: Sampooranta Divas of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji

events.ctx: The Guru Granth Sahib is the central religious scripture of Sikhism, regarded by Sikhs as the final, sovereign and eternal Guru.

title.gurmukhi: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਪੁਰਬ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ

title.roman: Jyoti-Jyot (Passing Away) of Guru Ram Das Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Ram Das Ji (1534-1581), the fourth Sikh Guru who founded the city of Amritsar. He passed away at Goindwal Sahib after serving as Guru for seven years, nominating his youngest son Guru Arjan Dev Ji as his successor.

title.gurmukhi: ਜੋਤੀ-ਜੋਤਿ ਗੁਰੂ ਅਮਰ ਦਾਸ ਜੀ
title.roman: Jyoti-Jyot (Passing Away) of Guru Amar Das Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Amar Das Ji (1479-1574), the third Sikh Guru who established Goindwal Sahib and strengthened the institution of Langar. He passed away at Goindwal Sahib after serving as Guru for 22 years, nominating his son-in-law Guru Ram Das Ji as his successor.

Annual Jormela at Gurdwara Kandh Sahib in Batala, Gurdaspur. Commemorates the holy marriage of Guru Nanak Dev Ji to Mata Sulakhni Ji in 1487 CE. The Gurdwara preserves the historic mud wall ('Kandh') beneath which Guru Nanak sat while an elderly woman warned him that the cracked wall would collapse upon him. Guru Nanak famously replied: 'Bhole Maai, eh Kandh sadiyan tak kayam rahegi' (O innocent mother, this wall shall stand for ages).

title.gurmukhi: ਜੋੜ ਮੇਲਾ ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ ਕੰਧ ਸਾਹਿਬ (ਬਟਾਲਾ)
title.roman: Jor Mela Gurdwara Kandh Sahib (Batala)

events.ctx: Commemorates the wedding of Guru Nanak Dev Ji to Mata Sulakhni Ji at Batala. The Guru's marriage established important Sikh traditions. Gurdwara Kandh Sahib in Batala marks the site where the wedding ceremony took place.

title.gurmukhi: ਵਿਆਹ ਪੁਰਬ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਦੇਵ ਜੀ (ਬਟਾਲਾ)
title.roman: Wedding Anniversary Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji (Batala)

events.ctx: Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Ram Das Ji as the 4th Sikh Guru.

title.roman: Gurgaddi Diwas Guru Ram Das Ji

events.ctx: Annual religious gathering at Gurdwara Tap Asthan Baba Budha Ji in Ramdas, Amritsar. Venerable Baba Budha Ji spent his final years here in deep prayer and meditation along the banks of the Ravi River. Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji traveled personally to Ramdas to serve Baba Budha Ji in his last hours and performed his cremation ceremonies with his own hands in 1631 CE.

title.gurmukhi: ਜੋੜ ਮੇਲਾ ਬਾਬਾ ਬੁੱਢਾ ਜੀ (ਰਾਮਦਾਸ)

events.ctx: Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Angad Dev Ji as the 2nd Sikh Guru.

title.hindi: गुरगद्दी दिवस गुरु अंगद देव जी

events.ctx: Foundation Day of the Singh Sabha Movement, launched on October 1, 1873 at Manji Sahib, Amritsar, under the leadership of Sardar Thakur Singh Sandhawalia, Baba Khem Singh Bedi, and Kanwar Bikrama Singh of Kapurthala. Born in response to Christian proselytization and Hindu assimilationist pressures, the movement spearheaded a magnificent renaissance in Sikh literature, historical scholarship, Punjabi education, and pristine Gurmat identity, culminating in the establishment of Khalsa College Amritsar.

title.gurmukhi: ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ ਲਹਿਰ ਸਥਾਪਨਾ ਦਿਵਸ
title.roman: Singh Sabha Movement Foundation Day

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Nanak Dev Ji (1469-1539), the founder of Sikhism and the first Guru. Before his passing at Kartarpur, he appointed Bhai Lehna (Guru Angad Dev Ji) as his successor, establishing the tradition of Guruship. His teachings of One God, equality, and truthful living continue to guide millions.

title.gurmukhi: ਜੋਤੀ ਜੋਤਿ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਦੇਵ ਜੀ
title.roman: Jyoti Jot Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
title.hindi: जोती-जोति श्री गुरु नानक देव जी

events.ctx: Annual religious gathering at Gurdwara Bir Baba Budha Ji in Thatha (Jhabal, Amritsar). It marks the sacred spot where Mata Ganga Ji, consort of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, walked on foot with simple Missi Roti, Lassi, and crushed onion to seek the blessings of venerable Baba Budha Ji, who blessed her that she would give birth to a warrior Guru who would crush oppressors like an onion, foreshadowing the advent of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji.

title.gurmukhi: ਜੋੜ ਮੇਲਾ ਬਾਬਾ ਬੁੱਢਾ ਜੀ (ਠੱਠਾ)
title.roman: Jor Mela Baba Budha Ji (Thatha)

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Harjinder Singh (Jinda) and Bhai Sukhdev Singh (Sukha), members of the Khalistan Commando Force who were hanged on October 9, 1992 in Yerwada Central Jail, Pune, for the assassination of General A.S. Vaidya, the Chief of Army Staff who commanded Operation Blue Star in June 1984.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਭਾਈ ਸੁੱਖਾ ਤੇ ਭਾਈ ਜਿੰਦਾ
title.roman: Shaheedi Bhai Harjinder Singh Jinda & Bhai Sukhdev Singh Sukha
title.hindi: शहीदी भाई सुक्खा व भाई जिंदा

events.ctx: Darbar Khalsa Dussehra represents the distinct Sikh tradition of celebrating the festival through martial vigilance, Shastar Puja (veneration of weapons as emblems of divine justice), and military exercises. Instituted during the era of the Sixth Guru Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib and fortified by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, Sikhs assemble at Takht Sri Hazur Sahib, Akal Takht, and Nihang Dal centres to recite Shastar Naam Mala and reaffirm their duty as Saint-Soldiers protecting the oppressed.

title.gurmukhi: ਦੁਸਹਿਰਾ (ਦਰਬਾਰ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਸ਼ਸਤਰ ਪੂਜਨ)

events.ctx: Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Har Krishan Ji as the 8th Sikh Guru.

title.roman: Gurgaddi Diwas Guru Har Krishan Ji
title.hindi: गुरगद्दी दिवस गुरु हरि कृष्ण जी

title.roman: Jyoti-Jyot (Passing Away) of Guru Har Rai Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Har Rai Ji (1630-1661), the seventh Sikh Guru known for his compassion and healing abilities. He passed away at Kiratpur Sahib, nominating his younger son Guru Har Krishan Ji as his successor at the age of five.
Guru Ram Das Ji (1534-1581) was the fourth Sikh Guru who founded the city of Amritsar, which became the spiritual center of Sikhism.

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Gobind Singh Ji (1666-1708), the tenth and final human Sikh Guru who established the Khalsa. Before his passing at Nanded (Hazur Sahib), he declared Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the eternal Guru of the Sikhs.

Saka Panja Sahib (1922) commemorates the sacrifice of Sikhs at Hasan Abdal (Panja Sahib). When a train carrying arrested Akali leaders passed by, Sikhs lay on the tracks to stop it and provide food and water. The train stopped, but many Sikhs were killed or injured. Their sacrifice remains a symbol of devotion to the Sangat.

title.gurmukhi: ਸਾਕਾ ਪੰਜਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ
title.roman: Saka Panja Sahib

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Beant Singh, who on October 31, 1984, assassinated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi following the catastrophic military invasion and desecration of Sri Harmandir Sahib and Sri Akal Takht Sahib during Operation Blue Star. He was shot and martyred immediately thereafter by Indo-Tibetan Border Police personnel in New Delhi.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਭਾਈ ਬੇਅੰਤ ਸਿੰਘ
title.roman: Shaheedi Bhai Beant Singh

events.ctx: Punjabi Suba Divas marks the creation of modern Punjab on November 1, 1966. Achieved through a 19-year non-violent mass movement led by the Shiromani Akali Dal under leaders including Master Tara Singh and Sant Fateh Singh, hundreds of thousands of Sikhs courted arrest demanding a Punjabi-speaking state with Gurmukhi as its official language. The struggle successfully led to the reorganization of East Punjab.

title.gurmukhi: ਪੰਜਾਬੀ ਸੂਬਾ ਦਿਵਸ
title.roman: Punjabi Suba Divas

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Mata Sahib Kaur Ji, the spiritual mother of the Khalsa.

title.gurmukhi: ਜਨਮ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਮਾਤਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਕੌਰ ਜੀ (ਖ਼ਾਲਸੇ ਦੀ ਮਾਤਾ)
title.roman: Prakash Diwas Mata Sahib Kaur Ji
title.hindi: जन्म दिवस माता साहिब कौर जी

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Bhagat Namdev Ji (1270–1350), an eminent saint-poet from Maharashtra whose 61 sacred hymns are enshrined across 18 Ragas in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Born into a calico-printer family, Namdev Ji's hymns celebrate intimate, ecstatic devotion to the Almighty, narrating how the Divine turned the temple of Dehra for him when Brahmins turned him away because of his low caste, asserting that the Lord belongs equally to all.

title.gurmukhi: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਭਗਤ ਨਾਮਦੇਵ ਜੀ
title.roman: Prakash Diwas Bhagat Namdev Ji

events.ctx: Bandi Chhor Divas (Day of Liberation) celebrates Guru Hargobind Ji's release from Gwalior Fort in 1619 along with 52 Hindu Rajas. The Guru refused to leave unless all 52 princes were also freed. Using a clever arrangement with 52 tails on his coat, all were liberated. This day coincides with Diwali and symbolizes the triumph of freedom over oppression.

title.gurmukhi: ਬੰਦੀ ਛੋੜ ਦਿਵਸ (ਦੀਵਾਲੀ)
title.roman: Bandi Chhor Divas (Diwali)

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sant Kartar Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale (1932–1977), the 13th Jathedar of the Damdami Taksal. A fearless preacher of Gurmat and ascetic scholar, he organized 37 massive Nagar Kirtans across Punjab during the Indira Gandhi Emergency to defy state repression and fearlessly awaken the Sikh youth to the ideals of the Khalsa.

title.gurmukhi: ਜਨਮ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਸੰਤ ਕਰਤਾਰ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ ਭਿੰਡਰਾਂਵਾਲੇ
title.roman: Birth of Sant Kartar Singh Bhindranwale
title.hindi: जन्म दिवस संत करतार सिंह भिंडरावाले

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Baba Budha Ji (1506–1631), born in Kathu Nangal, Amritsar. One of the most venerated figures in Sikh history, he was blessed as a young boy by Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Baba Budha Ji had the supreme honor of serving the first six Sikh Gurus and performing the ceremonial Gurgaddi tilak (coronation) for five Gurus (from Guru Angad Dev Ji to Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji). He was appointed the first Granthi of Sri Harmandir Sahib upon the first Parkash of the Adi Granth in 1604.

title.gurmukhi: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਬਾਬਾ ਬੁੱਢਾ ਜੀ
title.roman: Prakash Diwas Baba Budha Ji

events.ctx: Antim Sanskar (Cremation Day) of Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia (1718-1783), the leader of the Ahluwalia Misl who played a crucial role in Sikh military campaigns, including the capture of Lahore from Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces in 1761.

title.gurmukhi: ਅਕਾਲ ਚਲਾਣਾ ਸਰਦਾਰ ਜੱਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਆਹਲੂਵਾਲੀਆ
title.roman: Death Anniversary Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Baba Deep Singh Ji (1682–1757), revered Sikh scholar, copyist of Sri Guru Granth Sahib, and the first Jathedar of Damdami Taksal and Shaheedan Misl. In November 1757, learning that Afghan commander Jahan Khan had desecrated Sri Harmandir Sahib and filled the sacred Sarovar, 75-year-old Baba Deep Singh Ji led a band of Khalsa warriors to liberate the holy shrine. In the fierce Battle of Amritsar, even after receiving a mortal neck wound, he fought onward wielding his heavy Khanda until reaching the Parikrama of Sri Harmandir Sahib, fulfilling his solemn vow.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਬਾਬਾ ਦੀਪ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
title.roman: Shaheedi Diwas Baba Deep Singh Ji
title.hindi: शहीदी दिवस बाबा दीप सिंह जी

events.ctx: Foundation Day of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), inaugurated on November 15, 1920 at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar. Formed during the historic Gurdwara Reform Movement (Akali Tehreek) to free historical Gurdwaras from corrupt hereditary Mahants and British interference, the 175-member committee was tasked with managing shrines under strict Gurmat principles, later statutorily enacted via the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼੍ਰੋਮਣੀ ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਬੰਧਕ ਕਮੇਟੀ (SGPC) ਸਥਾਪਨਾ ਦਿਵਸ
title.roman: SGPC Foundation Day

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Shaheed Kartar Singh Sarabha (1896–1915), born in Sarabha village, Ludhiana. One of the most electrifying young revolutionaries of the Ghadar Party, he managed the revolutionary newspaper 'The Ghadar' in San Francisco before returning to Punjab to orchestrate an armed revolt against the British Raj among Indian soldiers. Betrayed by an informant, he was arrested and hanged in Lahore Central Jail on November 16, 1915 at only 19 years of age, becoming the legendary role model for Bhagat Singh.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਸ਼ਹੀਦ ਕਰਤਾਰ ਸਿੰਘ ਸਰਾਭਾ
title.roman: Shaheedi Diwas Shaheed Kartar Singh Sarabha
title.hindi: शहीदी दिवस शहीद करतार सिंह सराभा

events.ctx: Antim Sanskar (Cremation Day) of Bhai Mardana Ji (1459-1539), the lifelong companion of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. A Muslim by birth, he accompanied the Guru on all four Udasis (journeys) and played the Rabab while the Guru sang divine hymns. He was one of the first Sikhs and a model of devotion.

title.gurmukhi: ਅਕਾਲ ਚਲਾਣਾ ਭਾਈ ਮਰਦਾਨਾ ਜੀ
title.roman: Passing of Bhai Mardana Ji

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sahibzada Zorawar Singh Ji. Third son of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, martyred at Sirhind (1696-1705).

title.gurmukhi: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦਾ ਜ਼ੋਰਾਵਰ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
title.roman: Prakash Diwas Sahibzada Zorawar Singh Ji

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Nihang Baba Gurbaksh Singh Ji (1688–1764). During the seventh Afghan invasion in December 1764, Ahmad Shah Abdali marched upon Amritsar with 30,000 troops. Baba Gurbaksh Singh, along with a committed band of only 30 Nihang Singhs, stood guard outside Sri Darbar Sahib. Choosing martyrdom over surrender, they charged the Afghan vanguard near the Akal Takht, battling to their last breath to protect the dignity and sanctity of Sri Harmandir Sahib.

events.ctx: Foundation Day of the Shiromani Akali Dal, established on December 14, 1920 at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, as the task force of the Panth during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Dedicated to liberating historic Gurdwaras from corrupt Mahants through non-violent agitation, the Akali Dal unified regional Jathas under a single leadership (with S. Sarmukh Singh Jhabal as its first president) and went on to play a pivotal role in India's independence struggle.

events.ctx: Sis Ganj Sahib commemorates the site where Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's severed head was cremated by Bhai Jaita Ji after retrieving it from Delhi. Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Anandpur Sahib marks this sacred location, representing the Guru's supreme sacrifice for religious freedom.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੀਸ ਸਸਕਾਰ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ਼ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ (ਅਨੰਦਪੁਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ)

events.ctx: Commemorates the evacuation of Anandpur Sahib by Guru Gobind Singh Ji and the Sikhs in December 1705, after a prolonged siege by Mughal and hill forces. Despite promises of safe passage, the Sikhs were attacked upon leaving, leading to the battles of Chamkaur and Muktsar.

title.gurmukhi: ਕਿਲ੍ਹਾ ਅਨੰਦਗੜ੍ਹ ਛੱਡਣਾ (ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ)

events.ctx: Commemorates the separation of Guru Gobind Singh Ji's family at Sirsa during the evacuation of Anandpur Sahib in December 1705. Mata Gujri Ji and the younger Sahibzadas were separated from the Guru and later betrayed to the Mughal governor of Sirhind, leading to their martyrdom.

title.gurmukhi: ਪਰਿਵਾਰ ਵਿਛੋੜਾ (ਸਰਸਾ ਨਦੀ)
title.roman: Parivar Vichhoda (Sirsa River)

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas of Baba Jeevan Singh Ji (formerly Bhai Jaita Ji, 1649–1705). Following the public martyrdom of the Ninth Guru, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, in Chandni Chowk, Delhi (1675), Bhai Jaita performed the perilous feat of retrieving the Guru's sacred head (Sis) and carrying it across hundreds of miles to Sri Anandpur Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh Ji embraced him, proclaiming 'Ranghreta Guru Ka Beta' (Ranghreta is the Son of the Guru). He was initiated into the Khalsa Panth as Baba Jeevan Singh, trained Khalsa warriors, commanded the rear guard during the evacuation of Anandpur at Sarsa river, and fell fighting valiantly at the Battle of Chamkaur.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਬਾਬਾ ਜੀਵਨ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ (ਭਾਈ ਜੈਤਾ ਜੀ)

title.hindi: शहीदी दिवस बाबा जीवन सिंह जी

events.ctx: The martyrdom of the Elder Sahibzadas, Baba Ajit Singh Ji and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, occurred at the Battle of Chamkaur. Outnumbered 1 to 100,000, they fought with unprecedented valor. With their father Guru Gobind Singh Ji watching from the fortress, they entered the battlefield one after the other and attained martyrdom, proving that the Khalsa spirit is invincible even against overwhelming odds.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਵੱਡੇ ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ (ਬਾਬਾ ਅਜੀਤ ਸਿੰਘ ਤੇ ਬਾਬਾ ਜੁਝਾਰ ਸਿੰਘ)
title.roman: Shaheedi Elder Sahibzadas (Chamkaur Sahib)

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Sangat Singh Ji, a devoted Sikh commander whose appearance closely resembled Guru Gobind Singh Ji. At the historic Battle of Chamkaur (December 1705), when the fortress was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of imperial troops, the Panj Pyare ordered Guru Gobind Singh Ji to depart so the Khalsa Panth could live on. Bhai Sangat Singh was placed in command, donning the Guru's Kalgi (plume) and royal Choga. Standing on the ramparts of Chamkaur Garhi, he kept the enemy forces engaged until his glorious martyrdom, ensuring the Guru's safe passage.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਭਾਈ ਸੰਗਤ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ (ਚਮਕੌਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ)
title.roman: Shaheedi Bhai Sangat Singh Ji
title.hindi: शहीदी दिवस भाई संगत सिंह जी

events.ctx: The martyrdom of the Chotte Sahibzade (Sahibzada Zorawar Singh Ji and Sahibzada Fateh Singh Ji) and their grandmother, Mata Gujri Ji, is a unique and incomparable event in world history. Sentenced to be bricked alive for refusing to renounce their faith, the young Sahibzadas (aged 9 and 6) stood steadfast. They were martyred at Sirhind, while Mata Gujri Ji breathed her last in the Thanda Burj (Cold Tower). Their sacrifice shook the foundations of the Mughal Empire.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਛੋਟੇ ਸਾਹਿਬਜ਼ਾਦੇ ਤੇ ਮਾਤਾ ਗੁਜਰੀ ਜੀ (ਫ਼ਤਹਿਗੜ੍ਹ ਸਾਹਿਬ)

events.ctx: Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Satwant Singh and Bhai Kehar Singh, who were hanged on January 6, 1989 in Tihar Jail, New Delhi, for their involvement in the October 31, 1984 assassination of Indira Gandhi following the military assault on Sri Darbar Sahib. Their mortal remains were cremated inside the jail premises without being handed over to their families.

events.ctx: Commemorates the laying of the foundation stone of Sri Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar on 1 Magh 1645 Bk (December 1588). In an extraordinary testament to universal brotherhood and the inclusive spirit of Sikhi, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji invited the venerated Sufi saint of Lahore, Hazrat Sai Mian Mir Ji, to lay the foundation brick. Designed with four entrances open to all directions, castes, and creeds, it stands as the timeless spiritual center of the Sikh faith.

events.ctx: Maghi Mela at Muktsar is an annual religious fair held on Magh 1 (January 14) commemorating the Battle of Muktsar (1705) and the martyrdom of the Chaali Mukte (40 Liberated Ones). Thousands of devotees gather to take a holy dip and pay respects at Gurdwara Sri Muktsar Sahib.

title.gurmukhi: ਮਾਘੀ ਮੇਲਾ ਮੁਕਤਸਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ (ਚਾਲੀ ਮੁਕਤੇ)
title.roman: Maghi Mela Muktsar Sahib (40 Mukte)

events.ctx: Chabiyan Da Morcha (Keys Agitation) of 1922 was a peaceful protest during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Sikhs demanded the keys to the treasury of Harmandir Sahib from the British-appointed manager. Through non-violent resistance and negotiations, the keys were eventually returned to the Panth, marking a significant victory.

title.gurmukhi: ਚਾਬੀਆਂ ਦਾ ਮੋਰਚਾ
title.roman: Chabiyan Da Morcha

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Baba Deep Singh Ji (January 26, 1682 – November 11, 1757), born in Pahuwind village, Amritsar. A foremost disciple of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, he mastered Gurmukhi, Persian, Arabic, and martial warfare. He assisted Bhai Mani Singh Ji in preparing handwritten saroops of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Talwandi Sabo (Damdama Sahib) and founded the Taksal's exegetical and scholarly tradition.

title.gurmukhi: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਬਾਬਾ ਦੀਪ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
title.roman: Prakash Diwas Baba Deep Singh Ji
title.hindi: जन्म दिवस बाबा दीप सिंह जी

events.ctx: The Vaddha Ghallughara (Great Massacre) took place in February 1762. The Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali, determined to crush the rising power of the Sikhs, launched a surprise attack on a large gathering of Sikhs (Vahir) moving near Kup Rohira. The Sikhs, caught in an open plain with their families, formed a protective ring around the women, children, and elderly. In a single day of brutal fighting, an estimated 25,000 to 30,000 Sikhs achieved martyrdom. Despite this catastrophic loss, the Khalsa spirit remained unbroken, and they were able to liberate Punjab within a few years.

title.roman: Vaddha Ghallughara (Great Holocaust 1762)

events.ctx: Commemorates the wedding of Guru Gobind Singh Ji. The Guru was married to Mata Jito Ji (also known as Mata Sundri), and Mata Sahib Kaur Ji who became the spiritual mother of the Khalsa. These marriages took place at Anandpur Sahib.

title.gurmukhi: ਵਿਆਹ ਪੁਰਬ ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ
title.roman: Wedding Anniversary Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji

events.ctx: Basant Panchami in Sikh tradition marks the arrival of spring and is celebrated with profound spiritual fervor, notably at Gurdwara Chheharta Sahib near Amritsar. Guru Arjan Dev Ji constructed the historic six-wheeled well (Chheharta) here to alleviate water scarcity, around which the community gathered. Kirtan is traditionally recited in Raga Basant from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, symbolizing spiritual blossoming and renewal.

title.roman: Basant Panchami

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sahibzada Ajit Singh Ji. The eldest son of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, martyred at the Battle of Chamkaur (1687-1705).

events.ctx: Guru Har Rai Ji (1630-1661) was the seventh Sikh Guru known for his compassion and service to humanity regardless of their religion.

title.gurmukhi: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਗੁਰਪੁਰਬ ਗੁਰੂ ਹਰਿ ਰਾਇ ਜੀ

events.ctx: Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Bhagat Ravidas Ji, a visionary 15th-century socio-religious poet-saint from Varanasi. His 41 divine hymns across 16 Ragas in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji articulated the immortal concept of 'Begumpura' (the City without Sorrow)—an egalitarian society completely devoid of caste prejudice, exploitation, taxes, and tyranny. His life exemplified dignity of labor and spiritual supremacy through pure inner devotion.

title.gurmukhi: ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ ਦਿਹਾੜਾ ਭਗਤ ਰਵਿਦਾਸ ਜੀ
title.roman: Prakash Diwas Bhagat Ravidas Ji

events.ctx: Saka Nankana Sahib refers to the massacre that took place at Gurdwara Janam Asthan in February 1921. At the time, many Gurdwaras were controlled by corrupt Mahants. A group of peaceful Sikh reformers (Akalis), led by Bhai Lachhman Singh Dharowali, entered the Gurdwara to reclaim it. The Mahant, Narain Das, and his mercenaries attacked the peaceful group with guns and hatchets, killing over 130 Sikhs and burning their bodies. This sacrifice played a pivotal role in the Gurdwara Reform Movement, eventually leading to the formation of the SGPC and the liberation of historical Gurdwaras.

title.gurmukhi: ਸਾਕਾ ਨਨਕਾਣਾ ਸਾਹਿਬ (ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ ਜਥਾ ਭਾਈ ਲਛਮਣ ਸਿੰਘ)
title.roman: Saka Nankana Sahib

events.ctx: The Jaito da Morcha (1923-25) was a significant non-violent protest for religious freedom and the restoration of the deposed Maharaja of Nabha, Ripudaman Singh, a supporter of the Akali movement. Peaceful batches of Sikhs (Jathas) marched towards Jaito to hold an Akhand Path (continuous scripture reading). They were met with brutal force by British-led troops, resulting in many casualties. The movement eventually led to the passage of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act in 1925, bringing Gurdwaras under community control.

title.gurmukhi: ਜੈਤੋ ਦਾ ਮੋਰਚਾ
title.roman: Jaito Da Morcha

events.ctx: Marks the completion and first installation (Pehla Parkash) of the Adi Granth at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604 CE. Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled the sacred hymns of the first five Gurus, fifteen Bhagats, eleven Bhatts, and Gursikhs, sanctifying the shrine as the dwelling place of the Word of God. Revered Baba Budha Ji was appointed the first Granthi, carrying the sacred Scripture on his head with Guru Arjan Dev Ji waving the Chaur Sahib.

title.gurmukhi: ਸ੍ਰੀ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰ ਸ਼ਹਿਰ ਸਥਾਪਨਾ ਦਿਵਸ
title.roman: Foundation of Sri Amritsar City

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Chet (mid-March to mid-April), the first month of the Nanakshahi year and the arrival of Vasant Ritu (spring). Nature awakens as wild meadows bloom with colorful flowers, fresh tender leaves sprout, and bumblebees hum joyfully amidst the blossoms. In Barah Maha (Raag Tukhari), Guru Nanak Dev Ji depicts Chet as a delightful season when forests bloom across the wilds ('ਚੇਤੁ ਬਸੰਤੁ ਭਲਾ ਭਵਰ ਸੁਹਾਵੜੇ॥ ਬਨ ਫੂਲੇ ਮੰਝ ਬਾਰਿ'), teaching that the soul truly blossoms when the Beloved Lord returns to dwell within the heart. In Raag Majh, Guru Arjan Dev Ji proclaims that meditating upon Govind in Chet brings overflowing divine bliss ('ਚੇਤਿ ਗੋਵਿੰਦੁ ਅਰਾਧੀਐ ਹੋਵੈ ਅਨੰਦੁ ਘਣਾ').

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਚੇਤ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Chet

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Vaisakh (mid-April to mid-May), the second month of the Nanakshahi year, heralding the golden harvest across the plains of Punjab. Bountiful wheat fields ripple like an ocean of gold under warm morning skies as farmers reap their blessings. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji portrays Vaisakh as a sublime time when branches put on their fresh garments ('ਵੈਸਾਖੁ ਭਲਾ ਸਾਖਾ ਵੇਸ ਕਰੇ'), while the soul-bride waits at the Divine door longing for grace. Guru Arjan Dev Ji reflects on the sorrow of separation from the Beloved Lord amidst worldly illusions ('ਵੈਸਾਖਿ ਧੀਰਨਿ ਕਿਉ ਵਾਢੀਆ ਜਿਨਾ ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਬਿਛੋਹੁ'), reminding seekers that true fruition lies in communion with the Eternal Friend.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਵੈਸਾਖ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Vaisakh

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Jeth (mid-May to mid-June), the third month of the Nanakshahi calendar and the onset of intense summer heat (Grishma Ritu). The sun burns brightly high in the heavens, shimmering heatwaves rise from the sunbaked earth, and travelers seek the cooling refuge of ancient banyan trees. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji describes how the earth blazes like an oven ('ਪਲਵਚਿ ਜਲੈ ਧਰਤੀ ਪਰਬਤ ਤਪਹਿ ਘਣੇਰੇ'), observing that without the coolness of the Lord's presence, true relief cannot be found. Guru Arjan Dev Ji teaches that in the scorching heat of Jeth, holding fast to the sanctuary of the Lord protects the seeker from all worldly burning and affliction ('ਹਰਿ ਜੇਠਿ ਜੁੜੰਦਾ ਲੋੜੀਐ ਜਿਸੁ ਅਗੈ ਸਭਿ ਨਿਵੰਨਿ').

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਜੇਠ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Jeth

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Harh or Asarh (mid-June to mid-July), the fourth month of the Nanakshahi year. This is the height of midsummer heat when the parched earth longs passionately for the monsoon, and towering pre-monsoon thunderclouds begin to build majestically on the distant horizon. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji vividly captures the blazing sun in the sky and the earth enduring fiery heat while cicadas chirp in the forest ('ਆਸਾੜੁ ਭਲਾ ਸੂਰਜੁ ਗਗਨਿ ਤਪੈ॥ ਧਰਤੀ ਦੂਖ ਸਹੈ ਸੋਖੈ ਅਗਨਿ ਭਖੈ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji teaches that the scorching fires of desire consume only those who forget the Life of the World to place their hopes in mortals ('ਆਸਾੜੁ ਤਪੰਦਾ ਤਿਸੁ ਲਗੈ ਹਰਿ ਨਾਹੁ ਨ ਜਿੰਨਾ ਪਾਸਿ'), whereas the devotee rests in tranquil peace.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਹਾੜ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Harh

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Sawan (mid-July to mid-August), the fifth month of the Nanakshahi calendar, celebrating the joyful arrival of the monsoon (Varsha Ritu). Heavy life-giving rains pour from dark thunderclouds, drenching the fertile soil and turning the countryside into a carpet of vibrant emerald green. Droplets glisten on leaves as peacocks spread their magnificent plumage and dance with delight. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji sings of the rains bursting into seasonal showers and lightning flashing across the heavens ('ਸਾਵਣਿ ਸਰਸ ਮਨਾ ਘਨ ਵਰਸਹਿ ਰੁਤਿ ਆਏ॥ ਬਿਜੁਲਿ ਚਮਕੈ ਤ੍ਰਸੈ ਜੀਉ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji reveals that the soul-bride truly blossoms when imbued with love for the Lord's Lotus Feet, drinking the nectar of the Naam ('ਸਾਵਣਿ ਸਰਸੀ ਕਾਮਣੀ ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਸਿਉ ਪਿਆਰੁ').

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਸਾਵਣ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Sawan

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Bhadon (mid-August to mid-September), the sixth month of the Nanakshahi year, marking the peak of the monsoon deluge. Rain falls in torrential sheets, completely submerging lush green paddy fields and filling natural ponds, streams, and rivers to overflowing ('ਜਲ ਥਲ ਨੀਰਿ ਭਰੇ'). In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji paints an unforgettable nocturnal scene of deep rainy darkness where frogs croak, peacocks call, and the rain-bird cries out 'Prio, Prio!' for the Beloved ('ਬਰਸੈ ਨਿਸਿ ਕਾਲੀ ਕਿਉ ਸੁਖੁ ਬਾਲੀ ਦਾਦਰ ਮੋਰ ਲਵੰਤੇ॥ ਪ੍ਰਿਉ ਪ੍ਰਿਉ ਚਵੈ ਬਬੀਹਾ ਬੋਲੇ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji reminds us that in the fullness of this rainy season, worldly attachments fade like passing clouds, and only love for the Divine Lord brings eternal immersion in peace.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਭਾਦੋਂ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Bhadon

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Assu (mid-September to mid-October), the seventh month of the Nanakshahi calendar, inaugurating the serene transition into autumn (Sharad Ritu). As the monsoon clouds recede, the skies open up into brilliant, clear azure blue, and tall white feathery Kash grass (wild pampas reeds) blooms gracefully along riverbanks and canals. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji notes how the white reeds bloom ('ਕੂਕਹ ਕਾਹ ਫੁਲੇ') and the soul turns with deep yearning towards the Divine. Guru Arjan Dev Ji expresses the overwhelming surge of spiritual longing that rises in Assu ('ਅੰਸੂ ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਉਮਾਹੜਾ ਕਿਉ ਮਿਲੀਐ ਹਰਿ ਜਾਇ'), where the heart thirsts for the vision of the Beloved in the calm and clarity of autumn.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਅੱਸੂ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Assu

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Katak (mid-October to mid-November), the eighth month of the Nanakshahi calendar, characterized by crisp autumn air and radiant moonlit nights (Sharad Ritu). The evening skies turn sparkling and tranquil, illuminating rural rivers and village courtyards where earthen lamps (deepaks) are lit during Bandi Chhor Divas. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji portrays how the lamp of intuitive truth burns steadily within the enlightened heart, leading to blissful union ('ਦੀਪਕੁ ਸਹਜਿ ਬਲੈ ਤਤੁ ਜਲਾਇਆ॥ ਦੀਪਕ ਰਸ ਤੇਲੋ ਧਨ ਪਿਰ ਮੇਲੋ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji counsels that one reaps the fruit of one's own deeds without blaming others ('ਕਤਿਕਿ ਕਰਮ ਕਮਾਵਣੇ ਦੋਸੁ ਨ ਕਾਹੂ ਦੇਇ'), and that remembering Parmesar dispels all inner darkness and spiritual illness.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਕੱਤਕ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Katak

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Maghar (mid-November to mid-December), the ninth month of the Nanakshahi calendar, ushering in the early winter season (Hemant Ritu). Across Punjab, fertile agricultural fields are carpeted with freshly sprouted emerald-green winter wheat shoots. Ethereal morning mists hover over the plains before breaking into the warm, comforting golden rays of the winter sun. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji describes Maghar as a sublime month to sing praises of the Divine and merge in the Lord's presence ('ਮੰਘਰੁ ਮਾਹੁ ਭਲਾ ਹਰਿ ਗੁਣ ਅੰਕਿ ਸਮਾਵਏ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji declares that wondrously beautiful are those souls who sit in divine communion with the Beloved Lord ('ਮੰਘਰਿ ਮਾਹਿ ਸੁਹੰਦੀਆ ਹਰਿ ਪਿਰ ਸੰਗਿ ਬੈਠੜੀਆਹ'), remaining warm in spirit even as winter begins.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਮੱਘਰ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Maghar

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Poh (mid-December to mid-January), the tenth month of the Nanakshahi calendar and the onset of deep winter (Shishir Ritu). Dense white fog (Dhund) and freezing morning frost (Tukhar) blanket the northern plains, while the sun rises as a soft, pale golden sphere through the mist. In Sikh history, Poh is revered with immense solemnity and gratitude for the supreme fortitude and martyrdoms of the Chhote Sahibzadas and Mata Gujri Ji at Sirhind and Chamkaur. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji observes the freezing frost drying the sap of forest and fields ('ਪੋਖਿ ਤੁਖਾਰੁ ਪੜੈ ਵਣੁ ਤ੍ਰਿਣੁ ਰਸੁ ਸੋਖੈ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji reassures that the biting frost cannot touch one held close in the Lord's loving embrace ('ਪੋਖਿ ਤੁਖਾਰੁ ਨ ਵਿਆਪਈ ਕੰਠਿ ਮਿਲਿਆ ਹਰਿ ਨਾਹੁ'), radiating supreme inner warmth.

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਪੋਹ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Poh

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Magh (mid-January to mid-February), the eleventh month of the Nanakshahi year, as late winter begins to relent under bright, crisp sunshine. The landscape of Punjab transforms into a breathtaking, endless sea of vibrant yellow mustard flowers (Sarson ke Khet) stretching to the horizon. Commemorating the Forty Liberated Ones (Chaali Mukte) at Maghi, pilgrims gather at sacred Sarovars. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji teaches that true purification occurs when one discovers the sacred pilgrimage shrine within one's own heart ('ਮਾਘਿ ਪੁਨੀਤ ਭਈ ਤੀਰਥੁ ਅੰਤਰਿ ਜਾਨਿਆ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji proclaims that the supreme cleansing bath is the dust of the holy congregation and meditation upon the Divine Name ('ਮਾਘਿ ਮਜਨੁ ਸੰਗਿ ਸਾਧੂਆ ਧੂੜੀ ਕਰਿ ਇਸਨਾਨੁ').

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਮਾਘ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Magh

events.ctx: Sangrand marks the first day of Phagan (mid-February to mid-March), the twelfth and culminating month of the Nanakshahi year, celebrating the awakening of spring and the festival of Hola Mohalla. Orchards of fruit trees burst into clouds of delicate pink and white blossoms, petals carpet the tender green grass, and balmy breezes bring songbirds back to the groves. In Barah Maha, Guru Nanak Dev Ji describes how the heart rejoices in pure divine love and ego is dissolved ('ਫਲਗੁਣਿ ਮਨਿ ਰਹਸੀ ਪ੍ਰੇਮੁ ਸੁਭਾਇਆ॥ ਅਨਦਿਨੁ ਰਹਸੁ ਭਇਆ ਆਪੁ ਗਵਾਇਆ'), concluding that all twelve months and seasons are sublime for one who abides in union with the Divine ('ਬੇ ਦਸ ਮਾਹ ਰੁਤੀ ਥਿਤੀ ਵਾਰ ਭਲੇ'). Guru Arjan Dev Ji describes Phagan as an outpouring of supreme bliss when the Beloved Friend reveals Himself in the soul ('ਫਲਗੁਣਿ ਅਨੰਦ ਉਪਾਰਜਨਾ ਹਰਿ ਸਜਣ ਪ੍ਰਗਟੇ ਆਇ').

title.gurmukhi: ਸੰਗਰਾਂਦ ਮਾਹ ਫੱਗਣ
title.roman: Sangrand Month Phagan
